passages.title: The night market
passages.text:
The night market on Akpakpava Road opens when the shops close. By eight o'clock the pavement has become a kitchen: charcoal glows under grills of suya and roasted plantain, pots of pepper soup steam beside pyramids of boiled groundnuts, and the air smells of smoke, onions and diesel from the generators that light the stalls. Office workers who left home at five in the morning stop here on their way back, not only because the food is cheap but because the market is the one place where a clerk and a director will stand shoulder to shoulder, waiting for the same woman to turn the same skewers.

The council has tried twice to close it, citing hygiene and traffic. Both attempts failed within a fortnight. The traders simply returned, and the customers with them; the inspectors, who ate there themselves, found it hard to be zealous. A more sensible approach has since emerged: the council now collects a small nightly levy, provides two waste skips and a water tanker, and looks the other way.

It is an untidy arrangement, and purists on both sides dislike it. But it feeds thousands, employs hundreds, and has produced, without anyone planning it, the most democratic dining room in the city.

passages.title: The lost art of letter-writing
passages.text:
My grandfather kept every letter he ever received in a tin trunk under his bed. When he died we found more than six hundred of them, tied in bundles by year: letters from his brother in the army, from a friend who had gone to study in London, from my grandmother during the two years they were engaged and living in different towns. Reading them, I was struck less by the news they contained than by the care with which it was told. Each letter began with enquiries about health and harvest, moved through its business in orderly paragraphs, and closed with greetings to a dozen named people.

Nobody writes like that now. We send messages of a line or two, dozens a day, and keep none of them. The speed is a blessing; a grandmother in Kaduna can hear of a birth in Lagos within the hour. But something has been lost with the slowness. A letter that would take a week to arrive was written by someone who had thought about what was worth saying. A message that arrives in a second is often written by someone who has not.

I do not suggest that we abandon our phones. I suggest only that once in a while we write something long enough to be worth keeping in a tin trunk.

passages.title: Counterfeit drugs
passages.text:
The tablets looked exactly right. The packaging carried the manufacturer's logo, a batch number and an expiry date two years away. Only the price gave them away: half what the pharmacy across the road was charging. The woman who bought them for her feverish child did not know that they contained chalk and a little paracetamol, and that the malaria they were supposed to cure would continue, unchecked, for another five days.

Fake medicines kill more people in Africa each year than road accidents, yet they attract a fraction of the attention. Part of the reason is that their victims rarely know what killed them; a child who dies of malaria after taking 'medicine' is recorded as a malaria death. Part is that the trade is enormously profitable and its punishments, where they exist, are light. A drug counterfeiter in some states faces a smaller fine than a driver who ignores a traffic light.

Technology now offers some defence. Scratch panels on genuine packs reveal a code which, sent by text message, confirms the product is authentic. But the system depends on buyers who know it exists and can afford the text. The deeper cure is cheaper: a market in which the real drug is not twice the price of the fake, and a law that treats the sale of chalk to a sick child as the crime it is.

passages.title: Aunty Rose's scholarship
passages.text:
Aunty Rose was not really my aunt. She was the woman who sold bread at the junction near our school, and she had adopted, in the loose way of Nigerian streets, every child who passed her table. She knew our names, our classes and, somehow, our results. A child who had done well would find an extra roll slipped into his bag; one who had failed would receive a long look and the words, 'Next term, eh?'

The year I sat the entrance examination for the federal school, my father lost his job. The fees for the first term were beyond us, and I had resigned myself to the local secondary school when Aunty Rose appeared at our door with an envelope. It contained the exact sum, in old notes that smelt of flour. She would not say where it had come from and refused every suggestion of repayment. 'When you are big,' she said, 'you will do it for somebody else.'

She died the year I graduated. At her funeral I counted eleven people who had received envelopes, though I suspect there were more. None of us had known about the others. Between us we now pay the school fees of twenty-three children in that town, and not one of them knows our names.

passages.title: On lateness
passages.text:
There is a joke in this country that Nigerians operate on 'African time', a private clock that runs an hour or two behind the one on the wall. Like many jokes, it conceals a cost. A meeting called for ten that begins at eleven-thirty has wasted ninety minutes of every person in the room, and the person who arrives last has, in effect, stolen that time from all the others.

Lateness is rarely about traffic, whatever the latecomer says. It is about power. The important man arrives last because he can; the junior arrives first because he must. In many offices the meeting does not start until the most senior person walks in, which means that the more senior one becomes, the less reason one has to be punctual. Habits formed this way flow downwards, until the office messenger, too, has learnt that ten o'clock means whenever he arrives.

Countries that have broken this habit did not do it through appeals to culture but through consequence. Meetings begin on time whether or not the chairman is present; latecomers find the door closed or the decision taken. When lateness stops being a display of importance and becomes merely an embarrassment, the private clock quietly resets itself.

passages.title: The last blacksmith
passages.text:
Baba Ogundipe is the last blacksmith in a town that once had forty. His forge, a low shed of blackened zinc behind the motor park, produces hoes, cutlasses and the curved knives that palm-wine tappers use, and he makes them exactly as his father did, with a hand-pumped bellows and a hammer whose handle has been replaced so many times that he cannot say how old it is.

The imported tools that put his rivals out of business are cheaper, and he does not pretend otherwise. His customers are the farmers who have learnt that a Chinese cutlass, bright and light, loses its edge in a season, while one of his, dull and heavy, will outlast its owner. They pay twice as much and come back once a decade, which, as he observes with a dry smile, is a poor business model but an honest one.

He has trained three apprentices. Two left for Lagos; the third, his grandson, works beside him and has begun to sell the knives online, photographed against a white sheet, to buyers in Europe who pay ten times the local price for what they call 'artisanal' blades. Baba Ogundipe finds the word amusing. 'They are farm tools,' he says. 'But if the white man wants to hang his hoe on the wall, let him pay for it.'

questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: The examination was a piece of cake for Funmi.
questions.A: Funmi found the examination very easy
questions.B: Funmi ate cake during the examination
questions.explanation: 'A piece of cake' = something very easy.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: It is high time the council fixed the road.
questions.A: The road is on high ground
questions.B: The council fixed the road at noon
questions.C: The council should have fixed the road long ago
questions.D: The road will soon be fixed
questions.explanation: 'It is high time' + past tense expresses that something is overdue.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: Mrs Eze wears the trousers in that house.
questions.A: Mrs Eze prefers to dress like a man
questions.B: Mrs Eze does the family laundry every week
questions.C: Mrs Eze sells trousers for a living
questions.D: Mrs Eze is the one who makes the decisions at home
questions.explanation: To 'wear the trousers' is to be the dominant partner, the one who takes the decisions in a household.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: The senator's resignation came out of the blue.
questions.A: The senator's resignation was completely unexpected
questions.B: The senator resigned because of the weather
questions.C: The senator resigned in a blue suit
questions.D: The senator resigned from the Blue Party
questions.explanation: 'Out of the blue' = suddenly and unexpectedly.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: Dapo has been burning the candle at both ends since the semester began.
questions.A: Dapo has been wasting candles at both ends
questions.B: Dapo has been studying by candlelight at night
questions.C: Dapo has been exhausting himself by working late and rising early
questions.D: Dapo has been setting fires in the hostel
questions.explanation: 'Burn the candle at both ends' = overwork oneself day and night.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: The witness spilled the beans under cross-examination.
questions.A: The witness dropped food in court
questions.B: The witness lied to the court
questions.explanation: 'Spill the beans' = reveal a secret.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: The manager gave the new clerk a dressing-down.
questions.A: The manager scolded the clerk severely
questions.B: The manager gave the clerk a set of new clothes
questions.C: The manager promoted the clerk to a new post
questions.D: The manager sent the clerk home early that day
questions.explanation: A 'dressing-down' is a severe reprimand.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: Chika passed with flying colours.
questions.explanation: 'With flying colours' = with great success.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The manager was ADAMANT that the deadline would not be extended.
questions.explanation: Adamant means refusing to change one's mind.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The road was IMPASSABLE after the storm.
questions.explanation: Impassable means impossible to travel along.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: His CANDID remarks embarrassed the chairman.
questions.explanation: Candid means truthful and straightforward.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The two accounts of the accident were CONTRADICTORY.
questions.explanation: Contradictory accounts oppose each other.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The soldiers were ordered to RETREAT.
questions.explanation: To retreat is to move back.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The auditors found several DISCREPANCIES in the accounts.
questions.explanation: A discrepancy is a difference between things that should match.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: She spoke with such ELOQUENCE that the crowd fell silent.
questions.explanation: Eloquence is fluent, persuasive speaking.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The government has pledged to ERADICATE polio.
questions.explanation: To eradicate is to destroy completely.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The villagers were HOSTILE to the surveyors.
questions.explanation: Hostile means unfriendly or antagonistic.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The old bridge is in a PRECARIOUS state.
questions.explanation: Precarious means not securely held; likely to fall.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The minister's statement was deliberately EVASIVE.
questions.explanation: Evasive means avoiding commitment or a direct answer.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The rumour spread with astonishing RAPIDITY.
questions.explanation: Rapidity means great speed; the rumour spread very quickly.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The old woman remained STOICAL throughout the ordeal.
questions.explanation: Stoical means enduring pain or hardship without complaint.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The judge described the crime as HEINOUS.
questions.explanation: Heinous means shockingly evil.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The two leaders reached an AMICABLE settlement.
questions.explanation: Amicable means friendly and without hostility.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The chief was known for his GENEROSITY to strangers.
questions.explanation: Generosity is the opposite of meanness/stinginess.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The road to the village is very ROUGH.
questions.explanation: Rough is the opposite of smooth.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The evidence against him was FLIMSY.
questions.explanation: Flimsy (weak, insubstantial) is opposed by solid/strong.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The teacher's explanation was very SUPERFICIAL.
questions.explanation: Superficial (shallow) is the opposite of thorough/profound.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The prices in that shop are EXORBITANT.
questions.explanation: Exorbitant (unreasonably high) is opposed by reasonable/moderate.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The bridge has been declared STRUCTURALLY SOUND.
questions.explanation: 'Sound' here means in good condition; the opposite is unsafe/defective.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The contract was signed VOLUNTARILY.
questions.explanation: Voluntarily (of one's own free will) is opposed by under compulsion.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The town's water supply is ABUNDANT during the rains.
questions.explanation: Abundant is the opposite of scarce.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: Her handwriting is remarkably LEGIBLE.
questions.explanation: Legible is the opposite of illegible/unreadable.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The witness gave a COHERENT account of events.
questions.explanation: Coherent (logically connected) is opposed by confused/incoherent.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The new manager is very APPROACHABLE.
questions.explanation: Approachable is the opposite of aloof/unapproachable.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The soil in this region is ARID.
questions.explanation: Arid (very dry) is opposed by moist/wet.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The company's profits have been DWINDLING.
questions.explanation: Dwindling (gradually decreasing) is the opposite of growing.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The boy's behaviour was DELIBERATE.
questions.explanation: Deliberate (intentional) is the opposite of accidental.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The old man was FRAIL after his illness.
questions.explanation: Frail is the opposite of robust/strong.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The principal, ____ I have great respect, retires next month.
questions.explanation: 'For whom I have great respect' — the preposition governs the object pronoun 'whom'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Not only ____ late, but he also forgot his books.
questions.explanation: After 'Not only' at the start of a sentence, subject and auxiliary are inverted.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The police ____ investigating the matter.
questions.explanation: 'Police' is a plural noun in English.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Many a student ____ failed for lack of preparation.
questions.explanation: 'Many a' + singular noun takes a singular verb.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: ____ of the two brothers is taller?
questions.explanation: 'Which' is used when choosing from a limited, known set.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: She is the ____ of the two sisters.
questions.explanation: The comparative is used for two.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: I wish I ____ harder last term.
questions.explanation: A wish about the past takes the past perfect.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: He asked me where ____.
questions.explanation: Reported questions use statement word order and back-shift.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The bag was too heavy for her ____.
questions.explanation: 'Too + adjective + to + infinitive'; no object pronoun is repeated.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: By this time next year, I ____ my degree.
questions.explanation: The future perfect describes an action completed before a future time.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Ade, no less than his brothers, ____ to blame.
questions.explanation: 'No less than' does not change the number of the subject 'Ade'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The number of accidents on that road ____ alarming.
questions.explanation: 'The number of' takes a singular verb (contrast 'a number of').

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: A number of students ____ absent today.
questions.explanation: 'A number of' takes a plural verb.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: If it ____ tomorrow, the match will be postponed.
questions.explanation: First conditional: present simple in the if-clause.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The man denied ____ the money.
questions.explanation: 'Deny' is followed by a gerund.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: He is used to ____ early.
questions.explanation: 'Be used to' + gerund (contrast 'used to wake').

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: ____ you study, ____ you will pass.
questions.explanation: 'The + comparative ..., the + comparative ...' pattern.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Neither of the answers ____ correct.
questions.explanation: 'Neither' as a pronoun is singular.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The doctor insisted ____ seeing the patient immediately.
questions.explanation: The verb 'insist' takes the preposition 'on' followed by a gerund: insisted on seeing.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: She congratulated him ____ his promotion.
questions.explanation: 'Congratulate someone on something'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The children were prevented ____ entering the hall.
questions.explanation: 'Prevent someone from doing something'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Kunle is indifferent ____ criticism.
questions.explanation: 'Indifferent' takes the preposition 'to': indifferent to criticism.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The suspect was acquitted ____ all the charges.
questions.explanation: A person is 'acquitted of' a charge (found not guilty); 'convicted of' follows the same pattern.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The meeting was put ____ because of the strike.
questions.explanation: The phrasal verb 'put off' means to postpone; the strike caused the meeting to be postponed.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The soldiers ____ the rebellion within a week.
questions.explanation: 'Put down' a rebellion = suppress it.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The child takes ____ his father in looks.
questions.explanation: 'Take after' = resemble a parent.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: I cannot ____ with his rudeness any longer.
questions.explanation: 'Put up with' = tolerate.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The firemen managed to put ____ the fire.
questions.explanation: 'Put out' a fire = extinguish it.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: He ____ a good impression at the interview.
questions.explanation: 'Make an impression' is the collocation.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The witness ____ an oath before giving evidence.
questions.explanation: The fixed collocation is 'take an oath' (also 'swear an oath'), never 'make' or 'do' an oath.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option to which the given sentence relates when the word in capitals is stressed: Ibrahim REPAIRED the generator yesterday.
questions.A: Did Ibrahim sell the generator yesterday?
questions.B: Did Musa repair the generator yesterday?
questions.C: Did Ibrahim repair the pump yesterday?
questions.D: Did Ibrahim repair the generator today?
questions.explanation: Stress on REPAIRED contrasts the action.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option to which the given sentence relates when the word in capitals is stressed: The children ate rice at the PARTY.
questions.A: Did the children eat beans at the party?
questions.B: Did the adults eat rice at the party?
questions.C: Did the children eat rice at home?
questions.D: Did the children cook rice at the party?
questions.explanation: Stress on PARTY contrasts the place.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option to which the given sentence relates when the word in capitals is stressed: My BROTHER won the scholarship.
questions.A: Did your brother win the lottery?
questions.B: Did your sister win the scholarship?
questions.C: Did your brother lose the scholarship?
questions.D: Did his brother win the scholarship?
questions.explanation: Stress on BROTHER contrasts the person.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option to which the given sentence relates when the word in capitals is stressed: Mrs Okoro teaches CHEMISTRY at the college.
questions.A: Does Mrs Okoro teach at the university?
questions.B: Does Mrs Okoro teach physics at the college?
questions.C: Does Mr Okoro teach chemistry at the college?
questions.D: Does Mrs Okoro study chemistry at the college?
questions.explanation: Stress on CHEMISTRY contrasts the subject.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option to which the given sentence relates when the word in capitals is stressed: The bus leaves at SIX every morning.
questions.A: Does the bus leave at seven every morning?
questions.B: Does the train leave at six every morning?
questions.C: Does the bus arrive at six every morning?
questions.D: Does the bus leave at six every evening?
questions.explanation: Stress on SIX contrasts the time.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option to which the given sentence relates when the word in capitals is stressed: Halima wrote the letter in HAUSA.
questions.A: Did Halima write the essay in Hausa?
questions.B: Did Halima write the letter in English?
questions.C: Did Fatima write the letter in Hausa?
questions.D: Did Halima read the letter in Hausa?
questions.explanation: Stress on HAUSA contrasts the language.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option to which the given sentence relates when the word in capitals is stressed: The governor visited the school LAST week.
questions.A: Did the governor visit the school this week?
questions.B: Did the governor visit the hospital last week?
questions.C: Did the commissioner visit the school last week?
questions.D: Did the governor close the school last week?
questions.explanation: Stress on LAST contrasts the time.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option to which the given sentence relates when the word in capitals is stressed: Ekaette BORROWED the book from the library.
questions.A: Did Ekaette borrow the book from a friend?
questions.B: Did Ekaette steal the book from the library?
questions.C: Did Ekaette borrow the magazine from the library?
questions.D: Did Ime borrow the book from the library?
questions.explanation: Stress on BORROWED contrasts the action (borrowed, not stole).

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word that rhymes with the word in capitals: HEAD
questions.explanation: 'Head' is /hed/, rhyming with 'said' /sed/.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word that rhymes with the word in capitals: GREAT
questions.explanation: 'Great' is /greɪt/, rhyming with 'gate'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word that rhymes with the word in capitals: SWORD
questions.explanation: 'Sword' is /sɔːd/ (silent 'w'), rhyming with 'board'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word that rhymes with the word in capitals: WOMB
questions.explanation: 'Womb' is /wuːm/, rhyming with 'boom'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word that rhymes with the word in capitals: AISLE
questions.explanation: 'Aisle' is /aɪl/ (silent 's'), rhyming with 'mile'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word that rhymes with the word in capitals: BURY
questions.explanation: 'Bury' is pronounced /ˈberi/, rhyming with 'very'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: In the following word, choose the option that has the correct stress pattern (the stressed syllable is written in capitals): education
questions.explanation: '-tion' words are stressed on the preceding syllable: e-du-CA-tion.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: In the following word, choose the option that has the correct stress pattern (the stressed syllable is written in capitals): biology
questions.explanation: '-logy' words are stressed two syllables before the ending: bi-O-lo-gy.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: In the following word, choose the option that has the correct stress pattern (the stressed syllable is written in capitals): develop
questions.explanation: de-VE-lop — second-syllable stress.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: In the following word, choose the option that has the correct stress pattern (the stressed syllable is written in capitals): secretary
questions.explanation: SE-cre-ta-ry — first-syllable stress in British English.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: In the following word, choose the option that has the correct stress pattern (the stressed syllable is written in capitals): mathematics
questions.explanation: '-ics' words are stressed on the preceding syllable: ma-the-MA-tics.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: In the following word, choose the option that has the correct stress pattern (the stressed syllable is written in capitals): responsibility
questions.explanation: '-ity' words are stressed on the syllable before: res-pon-si-BI-li-ty.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: The word 'object' as a VERB is stressed
questions.explanation: Noun OB-ject; verb ob-JECT.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: The word 'import' as a NOUN is stressed
questions.explanation: Noun IM-port; verb im-PORT.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: The word 'conduct' as a VERB is stressed
questions.explanation: Noun CON-duct; verb con-DUCT.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: In the following word, choose the option that has the correct stress pattern (the stressed syllable is written in capitals): agriculture
questions.explanation: A-gri-cul-ture — first-syllable stress.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: In the following word, choose the option that has the correct stress pattern (the stressed syllable is written in capitals): opportunity
questions.explanation: '-ity' words are stressed on the syllable before: op-por-TU-ni-ty.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: In the following word, choose the option that has the correct stress pattern (the stressed syllable is written in capitals): necessary
questions.explanation: NE-ces-sa-ry — first-syllable stress.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the letters in capitals: bUS
questions.explanation: 'Bus' has /ʌ/, as in 'but'; the others have /ʊ/.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the letters in capitals: fAce
questions.explanation: 'Face' has /eɪ/, as in 'fame'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the letters in capitals: pEArl
questions.explanation: 'Pearl' has /ɜː/, as in 'purse'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the letters in capitals: bOY
questions.explanation: 'Boy' has /ɔɪ/, as in 'boil'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the letters in capitals: hOUse
questions.explanation: 'House' has /aʊ/, as in 'how'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the letters in capitals: Sugar
questions.explanation: 'Sugar' begins with /ʃ/, as in 'shoe'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the letters in capitals: THat
questions.explanation: 'That' begins with voiced /ð/, as in 'there'; the others have /θ/.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the letters in capitals: pleaSure
questions.explanation: 'Pleasure' has /ʒ/, as in 'garage' (/ˈɡærɑːʒ/).

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the letters in capitals: Xylophone
questions.explanation: Initial 'x' in 'xylophone' is /z/, as in 'zebra'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the letters in capitals: siNG
questions.explanation: 'Sing' ends in /ŋ/ alone, as in 'singer'; 'finger' has /ŋg/.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word in which the letter 'b' is SILENT.
questions.explanation: In 'climb' the final 'b' is not pronounced.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word in which the letter 'w' is SILENT.
questions.explanation: 'Wrist' is pronounced /rɪst/.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word in which the letter 'l' is SILENT.
questions.explanation: 'Calm' is pronounced /kɑːm/.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word in which the letters 'gh' are pronounced /f/.
questions.explanation: 'Enough' ends in /f/; the others have silent 'gh'.
